note: Close, faithful rendering of the commentary on the three times of mind and the plantain simile; nothing of substance to correct.
The Tibetan verses are rendered faithfully, with the Sanskrit lines given as marked notes; no substantive errors.

errors.english: If the transformation possesses a distinction, one observes it as either rough or otherwise. One might think:
errors.why: The milk example (its transformation is seen as rough or otherwise) is part of the opponent's thought introduced by སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ, not the author's own statement standing outside it.

errors.english: just as a distinction in the cause of existence results only in a distinction in the effect
errors.why: ཇི་ལྟར་སྲིད་པ here means 'to whatever extent there is' a distinction in the cause; it is not 'the cause of existence (bhava)'.

note: Generally sound Pramāṇa rendering; one opponent's premise is detached from the objection, and one phrase is misread as 'cause of existence'.

errors.english: Even though I was shaken, I did not let go.
errors.why: The thing that was stirring is the harmer (anger), which the Bodhisattva did not let loose even while it stirred; he himself was not 'shaken'. The king's echoing question (རྣམ་པར་གཡོ་བཞིན་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་མ་བཏང་བ) has the same error: 'even while you were shaken'.

errors.english: When it arises in men who wish for harm,
errors.why: The verse says ill-wishers rejoice whenever anger arises (in oneself), not that the anger arises in the ill-wishers.

errors.english: But one is said to have abandoned it [note: referring to a false accusation of losing one's temper], then bad reputation arises
errors.why: The verse describes the person ruled by anger, whom others shun, so that ill repute arises for him. The note about a false accusation has no basis in the text.

note: Readable verse rendering of the Kṣānti story, but several clauses about who is stirred, who rejoices, and who is shunned are misconstrued.

errors.english: what is called substance consists of two types of meaning: the external object and the consciousness.
errors.why: Substance is defined as the conditioned entity (pot etc.) that can accomplish, without depending on anything else, the two kinds of purpose connected with the object and with cognition; substance is not divided into 'object and consciousness'.

fix.find: what is called substance consists of two types of meaning: the external object and the consciousness. These are the actual nature of conditioned things such as a flask, which arise from a collection of causes and conditions and can be established without depending on others.
fix.replace: what is called substance is the very entity of conditioned things such as a flask, which arise from a collection of causes and conditions and which, without depending on anything else, are able to accomplish the two kinds of purpose connected with the object and with cognition.

note: Accurate on observation and non-observation and on the sound/smell debate, but the definition of substance is mis-segmented.
Faithful rendering of the momentariness argument, including the variant-reading remark; only minor phrasing could be tightened.

errors.english: Because his words are encountered by noble beings, they are like those of a high-born person.
errors.why: སྐྱེས here is 'a gift/present': when he meets the noble, his words become like a gift (an offering that pleases them). It does not mean 'a high-born person'.

note: Generally faithful handling of the commentary's compound analyses; one simile is misread.

errors.english: it is reasonable to call it a collection that meets in a single object
errors.why: འདུ་བ here is the Vaiśeṣika category inherence (samavāya), inherence in a single object; it is not a 'collection'. The same error appears in 'not a collection within a single whole' and 'That which possesses the collection'.

fix.find: it is reasonable to call it a collection that meets in a single object
fix.replace: it is reasonable to call it inherence (samavāya) in a single object

note: Argument against the variegated whole is followed well, but samavāya is consistently rendered as 'collection'.

span_why: It opens with the king's 'Have you come to beg?' and the jester's 'Go to the ritual house for food', which are on the previous side.

errors.english: The king asked: Is the food something else? Speak!
errors.why: 'My food is something else' is the Rākṣasa's line (continuing སྲིན་པོ་ནས། བདག་གི་ from the previous side); the king says only 'Speak!'.

fix.find: The king asked: Is the food something else? Speak!
fix.replace: The Rakshasa said: My food is something else. The king said: Speak!

errors.why: རལ་གྲིའི་ལོ་མ is the blade of a sword, so the flesh is cut with a sword blade, not with 'sword-like leaves'.

errors.english: This body also belongs to the deity.
errors.why: ལྷ here is the queen addressing her husband the king (deva, 'my lord'), so the body belongs to her lord. It does not belong to 'the deity'.

note: The drama is mostly followed, but it takes in lines from the previous side, gives the Rākṣasa's line to the king, and misreads a few words.

errors.english: marked with the name of the regional governor
errors.why: དུམ་བུ་འཛིན་པ is the proper name of the wicked brahmin chaplain (Khaṇḍahāla of the Candakumāra story), not a 'regional governor'. The same applies to every later 'the governor'.

fix.find: the regional governor [note: literally: "the one who holds the portion," likely referring to a local official or the previous ruler]
fix.replace: Khaṇḍadhara [note: the king's brahmin chaplain, Pali Khaṇḍahāla]

errors.english:
Possessing virtuous qualities and noble intelligence, he became a highly respected and grave figure.

In some great individuals, even a slight trace of lowliness is prevented by their very birth.
errors.why: This is a general gnomic verse (qualities, not birth, make a person weighty; even high birth is made light by faults). It is turned into narrative prose about the prince, and its point about birth is inverted.

note: The narrative is followed, but the antagonist's name is translated as a title, and the gnomic verses are flattened into prose with their point blurred.
